## Recent Advances in Watermark Detection

Watermarking has offered an effective approach to distinguishing text generated by large language models (LLMs) from human-written text. However, researchers have identified key challenges and developed new detection methods.

### Key Challenges

The pervasive presence of human edits on LLM-generated text dilutes watermark signals, thereby significantly degrading detection performance of existing methods. Additionally, no work has considered the imperceptibility of watermarked LLMs, and LLM service providers may not disclose the existence of watermarks, as it could reduce user willingness to use the service and make it more vulnerable to attacks.

### Detection Methods

A new method called a truncated goodness-of-fit test (Tr-GoF) was introduced for detecting watermarked text under human edits. The Water-Probe algorithm has been developed for identifying watermarked LLMs by constructing two prompts with similar output distributions, then sampling repeatedly using two fixed watermark keys for each prompt, with watermark presence determined by comparing the similarity of distribution differences between the two prompts.

### Watermarking Schemes

The prominent family of Red-Green watermarks achieves detection by, at each step of generation, selecting a context-dependent pseudorandom set of logits to be boosted. Recently proposed families of Fixed-Sampling and Cache-Augmented schemes have focused on developing watermarks that aim to preserve the output distribution of the LLM.

### Toolkit Development

MarkLLM is an open-source toolkit for LLM watermarking that was presented as a demo at EMNLP 2024.

## Overview of Recursive Language Models (RLMs)

Recursive Language Models (RLMs) are a general inference framework for language models that offloads the input context and enables language models to recursively sub-query language models before providing an output.

## Key Research and Development

The major research publication "Recursive Language Models" was published in December 2025 by Alex L. Zhang, Tim Kraska, and Omar Khattab from MIT CSAIL. This research proposes a new inference strategy rather than a new neural architecture.

## How RLMs Work

The framework offloads context into a Python REPL environment as a variable in memory, enabling the language model to reason over its context in code and recursive LM calls, rather than purely in token space. The RLM allows the model to actively manage its own context.

## Performance and Applications

Results across multiple settings and models demonstrated that RLMs are an effective task-agnostic paradigm for both long-context problems and general reasoning. RLMs provide an elegant way to scale up the context window length of any LLM.

## Training Native RLMs

Training a native RLM involved supervised fine-tuning using curated datasets collected from RLM trajectories of larger models and distilled versions of smaller models, creating RLM-Qwen3-8B, the first natively recursive language model.

## BiScope: AI-generated Text Detection

BiScope addresses the pressing need to detect text generated by Large Language Models (LLMs) in order to identify and prevent misuse across various applications, including misinformation and academic dishonesty.

### Core Innovation

The key observation is that how well the current token's output logits memorizes the closely preceding input tokens provides strong evidence for AI-generated text detection. The researchers propose a novel bi-directional calculation method that measures cross-entropy losses between an output logits and the ground-truth token (forward) and between the output logits and the immediately preceding input token (backward).

### Performance Results

BiScope was evaluated on texts generated by five latest commercial LLMs across five heterogeneous datasets, including both natural language and code, demonstrating superior detection accuracy and robustness compared to six existing baseline methods, exceeding state-of-the-art non-commercial methods' detection accuracy by over 0.30 F1 score and achieving over 0.95 detection F1 score on average. It also outperforms GPTZero, a commercial tool based on a commercial LLM trained with enormous volumes of data.

CORAL (COnsistent RAnk Logits) is a framework with strong theoretical guarantees for rank-monotonicity and consistent confidence scores. CORAL is a method for ordinal regression with deep neural networks that addresses the rank inconsistency issue of other ordinal regression frameworks.

Cao et al. proposed the CORAL framework, which aims to avoid increasing the complexity of training by applying weight sharing in the penultimate layer of the neural network. I've found comprehensive information about synthetic data, iterative training of LLMs, and model collapse from 2024-2025. Here are the key findings:

## Model Collapse Phenomenon

Model collapse, sometimes referred to as "Model Autophagy Disorder," describes a degenerative process where successive generations of models exhibit progressively diminishing quality when trained on synthetic data produced by their predecessors.

## How It Manifests

Models iteratively fine-tuned on their own outputs gradually lose their ability to accurately model human text. Iterative self-tuning has been found to produce lower lexical, semantic, and syntactic diversity, with syntactic diversity experiencing the strongest decline.

Even one-round of training on synthetic data leads to significant increases in test perplexity, and as little as 1% of synthetic data in a training dataset can still lead to model collapse.

## Scope of the Issue

Recursive training on synthetic data causes irreversible defects across language models, vision models, and diffusion models. Three sources of error (statistical approximation, functional expressivity, functional approximation) compound across generations.

## Current Use and Benefits

Despite these risks, developers are increasingly turning to synthetic data generated by LLMs as an alternative to human-written text, and it is being used in both pre-training and post-training to produce capable models.

## Mitigation Strategies

Research shows that iteratively generating synthetic responses from the model while obtaining additional responses from an exogenous source and training the next generation with both types can help prevent collapse if the external signal contains correct responses.

## Overview

Ordinal regression, also known as ordinal classification, aims to solve classification problems in which categories are not independent but instead follow a natural order. Ordinal classification is a key task in natural language processing with many applications that require ordering or ranking in the output such as Sentiment Analysis, Rating Prediction, and Age Group Classification.

## Key Distinctions

Unlike normal classification, ordinal regression takes into account the natural ordering of categories in the response variable, which allows for more nuanced and accurate modeling when the order of categories carries meaningful information, as well as training a universal model to learn ordered information from different ordinal regression tasks jointly.

## 2024 Research Developments

Many real-world prediction problems have ordinal response variables, and conventional classification losses such as multi-category cross-entropy ignore this ordering information. Ordinal regression methods for deep neural networks address this.

Recent 2024 work includes the use of neural models for classifying English written exams into CEFR competence levels. Additionally, with the advent of Pretrained Language Models, it became possible to tackle ordinality through the implicit semantics of the labels as well, with comprehensive theoretical and empirical examination of both explicit and implicit approaches.

The field continues to explore specialized loss functions and neural architectures designed specifically to preserve and exploit the ordinal nature of classification tasks in NLP applications.

Model collapse is a compounding degenerative effect in the performance of models when recursively re-trained on synthetic data, where the self-consuming cycle gradually drives the model far from the true data-generating distribution.

Synthetic data are rarely used in raw form in practical applications; instead, practitioners often apply filtering steps to remove low-quality synthetic samples before retraining.

## Model Collapse Overview

Model collapse is a degenerative process caused by training on synthetic data from previous generations, leading to compounded errors and models that have converged to a low variance distribution that is significantly dissimilar to the original model trained on human data. ## Overview

"Self-Consuming Generative Models Go MAD" is a paper presented at ICLR 2024 that examines how advances in generative AI have led to the temptation to use AI-synthesized data to train next-generation models, creating an autophagous ("self-consuming") loop whose properties are poorly understood.

## Key Research

The research conducts analytical and empirical analysis using state-of-the-art generative image models of three families of autophagous loops that differ in how fixed or fresh real training data is available through generations of training and whether samples from previous-generation models have been biased to trade off data quality versus diversity.

Without enough fresh real data in each generation of an autophagous loop, future generative models are doomed to have their quality (precision) or diversity (recall) progressively decrease—a condition termed Model Autophagy Disorder (MAD), by analogy to mad cow disease, with appreciable MADness arising in just a few generations.

The research studied three types of realistic self-consuming loops: "fully synthetic loops," "synthetic augmentation loops" (where fixed real data is present), and "fresh data loops" (where new, unseen real data is present).
